reference.source: Campbell-Walsh-Wein Urology / WHO laboratory manual for semen analysis
clinicalPearls: Chronic epididymitis is persistent discomfort or pain localised to the epididymis, conventionally present for three months or more, often with a palpably firm or thickened epididymis
It is frequently non-infective and inflammatory or of uncertain cause, in contrast to acute epididymitis which is usually driven by sexually transmitted or urinary organisms
The pain may be constant or intermittent, is often dull and aching, and can radiate to the groin, lower abdomen, or perineum
Careful examination localises tenderness to the epididymis and helps exclude a testicular mass, and scrotal ultrasound supports assessment
A history of previous acute epididymitis, scrotal surgery, or vasectomy is common and may point to a post-inflammatory or obstructive congestive mechanism
Management is largely conservative and symptomatic, with reassurance, supportive measures, analgesia, and anti-inflammatory strategies rather than repeated courses of antibiotics
Antibiotics are appropriate only when active infection is demonstrated, and their reflexive prolonged use should be avoided
Refractory cases require careful multidisciplinary pain management, and surgery such as epididymectomy is a last resort with counselling about uncertain benefit
reference.pathophysiology: Chronic epididymitis denotes long-standing epididymal pain that in most cases is not due to ongoing infection. It may follow an episode of acute epididymitis, with residual inflammation, fibrosis, and scarring of the epididymal tubules, or arise from congestion and obstruction, as can occur after vasectomy. In many men no infective or structural cause is identified and the condition is best understood as a chronic inflammatory or neuropathic pain state involving sensitisation of scrotal afferent nerves. Coexisting or overlapping chronic pelvic pain and referred pain from the lower urinary or musculoskeletal structures frequently contribute. The distinction from acute infective epididymitis is important because it changes management away from antimicrobial therapy towards a chronic-pain approach.
additionalDifferentials: Chronic orchialgia and idiopathic chronic scrotal pain
Referred pain from ureteric calculus, inguinal hernia, or nerve entrapment
additionalInvestigations: Clinical examination to localise tenderness and exclude a testicular mass
Scrotal ultrasound to assess the epididymis and testis and detect cysts, varicocele, or tumour
Urine analysis and culture to identify or exclude urinary infection
Sexually transmitted infection screening where risk factors or urethral symptoms are present
Assessment for referred causes including abdominal, inguinal, and musculoskeletal examination
Review of previous scrotal surgery or vasectomy contributing to symptoms
redFlags: A discrete or hard testicular mass on examination or ultrasound requiring tumour exclusion
Acute severe pain with swelling suggesting torsion or superimposed acute infection
Systemic features of infection such as fever and rigors
reference.prognosis: The condition is benign but can be persistent and frustrating, with symptoms often waxing and waning; many men improve with conservative measures and time, though a subset have long-lasting pain that is difficult to abolish and requires ongoing pain-focused management.
pitfalls: Repeatedly prescribing antibiotics in the absence of proven infection
Overlooking a testicular tumour presenting as chronic scrotal discomfort
Failing to consider referred pain from the ureter, hernia, or entrapped nerves
Proceeding to surgery without realistic counselling about uncertain outcomes
Neglecting the psychological impact and the value of a chronic-pain approach
references: European Association of Urology guidelines on chronic pelvic pain
British Association of Urological Surgeons guidance on scrotal pain
management: Shift management away from repeated antibiotic courses, reserving antimicrobials only for microbiologically proven infection
Provide conservative symptomatic care with reassurance, scrotal support, local heat and activity modification
Treat pain with anti-inflammatory analgesia and, where a neuropathic component is evident, neuromodulatory agents such as amitriptyline or a gabapentinoid
Address contributing factors including post-vasectomy congestion, referred abdominal or musculoskeletal pain and overlapping chronic pelvic pain syndrome, with pelvic-floor physiotherapy
Consider spermatic cord nerve block for refractory pain, and epididymectomy only as a last resort after careful counselling
Refer to a chronic pain pathway or specialist andrology service and offer psychological support for persistent symptoms
